In this lesson, you will learn about operational amplifier circuits.
INTRODUCTIONM
Operational amplifiers contain a differential amplifier, common collector amplifier and a push-pull amplifier.
They always amplify the difference between the inverted and non-inverted inputs.
The way operational amplifiers are connected in a circuit determines the type of amplifier.
Let's begin the lesson on OPERATIONAL AMPLIFIER OPERATION...................

Inside are dozens of transistors, diodes and resistors.
Because the circuit is miniaturized and sealed in a package, access to internal circuitry is not possible.
Only the inputs, output and power supply leads are connected externally. The op-amp is treated as a single component.
External connections are shown by pin numbers. Use an op-amp reference book to determine pins and circuit connections.
Normally, the power supply connections are not shown in schematics. It is understood that op-amps require operating voltages..
The op-amp is a super transistor. It exhibits a nearvery large input resistance, zero output resistance, and near infinite voltage, current and power gain.{
The op-amp is a super transistor. It exhibits a near infinite
input resistance, zero output resistance, and a very large voltage, current and power gain...............
Op-amps amplify frequencies ranging from 0 Hz (DC) to several hundred kHz.
Because of these characteristics, op-amps are extremely unstable and need to be controlled.
Op-amps are controlled by external circuits that stabilize their operation using degenerative feedback. This is called closed loop mode of operation.

CLOSED LOOP MODE OF OPERATION - The closed loop mode uses feedback. The output is fed back to the input creating a loop. Op-amps, in special circuits, also use the open loop mode where no feedback signals are used.
Let's look at four op-amp circuits. First, the non-inverting amplifier.
This is a typical non-inverting amplifier. The input is applied to the + input of the op-amp.
Resistors Rf (feedback) and R1 form a voltage divider that applies part of the output signal to the inverting input.
Since the input and output signals are in phase, the result of applying the output signal to the inverting input produces degenerative feedback.
The amplifier amplifies the difference between the input and the feedback signal.
The degenerative feedback reduces the gain of the op-amp to a controllable amount.
Applying a DC input does not change circuit operation.
Gain is calculated by the ratio of the output resistance to input resistance:
For example, the gain of this non-inverting amplifier is 11.

Resistor Rf1 applies part of the output signal to the inverting input.
The feedback reduces the gain of the op-amp to a controllable amount.
Using DC inputs does not change circuit operation.
Differential amplifiers normally use a gain of 1. Rf1 and Rin(-) are equal.

Last, let's look at the summing amplifier circuit..........
This is a typical summing amplifier. Several inputs are applied to the - input of the op-amp.
Resistor Rf applies part of the output signal to the inverting input.
Since the input and output signals are out of phase, the result of applying the output signal to the inverting input produces degenerative feedback.
The degenerative feedback reduces the gain of the op-amp to a controllable amount.
Using DC inputs does not change circuit operation.
Summing amplifiers normally use a gain of 1.
The two external inputs produce a combined input to the op-amp.
The combined input is amplified by a gain of 1 and applied to the output.
What is the normal gain of summing amplifiers?
Summing amplifiers normally have a gain of 1...............

To determine normal operation, find the sum of the inputs and compare to the output.
Output = -(Input 1 + Input 2) = -(-5 V + +3 V) = +2 V
